source_title: Weak magnetic anomaly detection for defence and security - ISED Canada

Canada has a requirement for magnetic anomaly detection for defence and security. Traditional magnetometers, such as fluxgate sensors, have been used for decades to measure the strength and direction of magnetic fields. A fluxgate magnetometer is a relatively simple classical device: it consists of a coil of wire wrapped around a core material and detects changes in magnetic flux passing through the sensor. While reliable, these classical sensors face inherent limitations in size, sensitivity, accuracy, and long term stability. Quantum magnetometers, by contrast, leverage the principles of quantum mechanics and promise the ability to achieve superior performance. They offer enhanced sensitivity, improved accuracy and stability, and in some cases even reduced size and weight compared to their classical counterparts.
There is a lack of suitably mature quantum sensors in the commercial space. The government of Canada has identified a need to develop a device or system consisting of hardware and software and a quantum sensor or a mix of classical and quantum sensors capable of sensing nanotesla (nT) or even femtotesla (fT) magnetic signals that can be used for a myriad of commercial, medical, and defence applications. In scanning the research underway, there appears to be interest in various means for the sensing of magnetic fields, including but not limited to Superconducting Quantum Interference Devices (SQUID), Superconducting Quantum Interference Filter (SQIF), and (Nitrogen Vacancy (NV) diamond. In addition to this we are led to believe that Rydberg atoms, typically framed for electric field detection can be reconfigured and/or adapted for magnetic field detection as well. We are also aware of another technology termed Spin-Exchange Relaxation-Free (SERF) which is very sensitive, but so sensitive as to be problematic to employ. This investigation seeks to explore nT and even fT sensitivities.

The device must provide azimuth to +/- 5 degrees, and an inclination of +/- 5 degrees.

Specificity The device must be able to separate a target signal from background noise. A sensitive magnetometer will detect a plethora of magnetic fields in a given cluttered environment, but the user will be interested in the absence or presence of a target signal. The device must detect and identify three specific Steel 1018 ferromagnetic targets at a minimum distance of 10 meter through free space. It must achieve a 95% true positive rate (TPR) for both detecting the presence of a target and classifying which specific target is present.

Magnetometry and magnetic sensors play an important role in the detection and measurement of magnetic fields around us. Applications for use exist in many industries and interest areas are not limited to natural resource discovery (including critical minerals), monitoring of the environment, healthcare, defence, and security.
For natural resource discovery magnetic sensors are used to help sense and identify mineral deposits including copper, nickel, iron, and gold. Indeed, the same technology has promise in the search for rare earth minerals which are essential to commercial, academic, and security uses.
Magnetic sensors also play an important role in environmental monitoring. They can be used to track ocean currents, detect geologic activity, and observe other natural processes. By measuring subtle variations in magnetic fields and related proxy signals, magnetometers provide valuable insights into changes in the Earth’s climate.
In healthcare, many imaging technologies—most notably magnetic resonance imaging—depend on generating and detecting subtle perturbations in magnetic flux. Researchers are now exploring the use of nitrogen vacancy diamonds integrated into existing MRI systems, with the goal of achieving higher sensitivity and improved image resolution.
